narration: The team, led by palaeontologist Olivier Lambert, described the animal in 2010. They first named it Leviathan, after the sea monster of legend. But that name had already been given to another animal, an extinct relative of elephants, so the genus became Livyatan, the Hebrew form of the word. The species name, melvillei, honours Herman Melville, the author of Moby-Dick. A fitting tribute for a whale that may have hunted other whales.

narration: On top of the skull sits a deep hollow called the supracranial basin. In living sperm whales, a similar basin holds the spermaceti organ, so Livyatan probably had one too. What that organ did is still debated. It may have focused sound for echolocation, helping the whale find prey in murky water. Some researchers have even suggested it worked as a cushion for ramming, although that idea is controversial.

narration: One idea is that its menu changed. As the climate cooled towards the end of the Miocene, ocean ecosystems were reshaped. Many of the mid-sized baleen whales it relied on declined, while others grew larger. A specialist predator can struggle when its prey changes. Isolated teeth from places such as Chile, South Africa and Australia suggest giant raptorial sperm whales were once widespread, but in the end this lineage of whale hunters faded away.
